speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Before I start, I would like to declare my interest as both an art historian and the owner of a digital art magazine.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In that year, a man boldly walked up to the then-President of Singapore, Mr Ong Teng Cheong, at a major art event.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: That man spoke to the President briefly, the President nodded and the man proceeded to put on a jacket.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: That jacket had bright gold lettering on the back of it and that man was none other than Mr Tang Da Wu, one of Singapore's most celebrated artists, and the gold lettering on his jacket read, "Don’t Give Money to the Arts." Once the jacket was on, Tang passed the President a handwritten note which also said, "I am an artist.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I am important." This performance has entered into the annals of Singapore's art history.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As with many pieces of performance art, it is dripping with irony and wit.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The pointed message on the jacket about funding, contrasts with the genuine plea in the note that the artist is, in fact, important.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is a concern that was relevant in 1995 and continues to be relevant now.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This jacket now hangs in the National Gallery across the road and is part of Singapore's national art collection.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This artwork is perhaps one that immediately comes to mind – at least amongst Singapore art historians – when one thinks about the creative economy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In it, Minister Edwin Tong referred to a desire to "unlock Singapore's creative economy and to create good jobs." The term "creative economy" then goes on to appear more than 20 times in the body of the Arts Plan.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While there is no single definition of the "creative economy", the Arts Plan refers to the United Nations Committee on Trade and Development, which defines the creative economy as the intersection of human creativity and technology or products that have economic value.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Plan then elaborates that, "This includes a wide variety of sectors, such as architecture, design, fashion, film, music, performing arts and television." In Singapore, a tremendous amount of Government funding has been poured into the arts community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Under Singapore's law, charitable purposes, in respect of which charities may be constituted, include the advancement of the arts and heritage.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, while there are many for-profit arts businesses in the space, our legislative framework for charities and the practices of the Government lend support to the view that arts offerings are also public goods, which fulfill an important social aim.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Our creative economy relies both on private enterprise and public support.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As Minister Edwin Tong has said in his foreword to the Arts Plan, the arts have an important role in forging a connected society.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: He said, in particular, "Our social fabric is changing…  the arts have the power to unite our communities and anchor us to our core Singaporean identity." This very important role of the arts identified by the Minister is something I absolutely agree with and cannot emphasise more.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Considering the creative economy within this framework, which takes into account both the broader social impact of the arts as well its bread-and-butter concerns, I would like to highlight four areas in which more support can be rendered to assist artists and art entities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, more direct support can be put in place to assist creative workers, businesses and universities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a topic of pressing importance in the arts community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Just this past weekend, I attended a standing-room only panel discussion at 7879 Gallery & Clayworks.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a space where many arts workers came together to discuss how to build sustainable art careers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Government, undoubtedly, has a very important role to play as a facilitator of assistance and networking space for creative businesses in the arts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Our Arts Resource Hub and grant framework under NAC are excellent initiatives, but much more can be done.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It also works to connect potential investors with creative businesses, while educating arts entities to provide them with the necessary knowledge for securing various forms of investment – and these range from equity to debt and grants.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It would be very helpful to have a similar centralised networking portal in Singapore for arts entities in order to help such entities gain access to potential investors.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Our local context also offers signposts on how affordable professional services may be rendered to suitable arts businesses and charities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: With my own personal experience serving as a volunteer with the Pro Bono SG office, I can share that Pro Bono SG has achieved some success with its low-bono initiatives under its Family Justice Support Scheme.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here, legal representation at discounted rates is available for needy family law litigants who are not eligible for assistance from the Legal Aid Bureau.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The benefits of this scheme are clear – subsidised legal assistance is given based on need.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This creates greater access to justice but, at the same time, there is an element of sustainability, in that service providers are not left out-of-pocket either.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A scheme like this could help arts and cultural workers and arts businesses to be "match-made" with key service providers, such as lawyers, accountants, technology experts, human resources (HR) professionals, marketers and more.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Anyone who is willing and able to support the arts through the rendering of discounted services should be assisted with being given access to the entities that actually need this help.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These need to be supported as well, so that our arts institutions are well-equipped with high-quality staff and programmes.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: One example I would like to highlight today is the challenge that is presently being faced by the Nanyang Academy of Fine Arts (NAFA).

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: NAFA is one of the founding members of the newly launched University of the Arts Singapore (UAS).

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Young autonomous universities, like the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) and Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), are able to receive Government matching on public donations in ratios that can go well beyond simple dollar-for-dollar amounts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: NAFA, being a private institution under UAS, does not enjoy the same privileges.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, NAFA seeks dollar-for-dollar matching assistance for donations through the Cultural Matching Fund (CMF) and this is something that is overseen by the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY).

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Since 2022, CMF rules have become much more restrictive.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: What this means is that, in the last few years, NAFA has not been able to benefit fully from direct donation matching under CMF.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I also understand that this situation creates a disincentive for private donors to donate to the institution.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is because their donations are likely to have a bigger overall impact, if applied to, say, autonomous universities instead, where private donations will be matched in higher ratios by the Government.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The issue here is a simple one: without good and well-funded arts schools, we will not be able to produce good artists and cultural producers who are the very backbone of our creative economy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, I would like to address how we can do more to align the development of our arts sector with Singapore's larger economic goals and, in particular, with respect to our tax policies.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The first area I would like to highlight is in connection with the Goods and Services Tax (GST).

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Earlier this month, the hon Member Mr Sitoh Yih Pin talked about the GST "cow" being milked as a political tool, and I can assure this House that I have no intention of doing that today.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: All I would like to do is highlight that, in Singapore, we do not include the supply of artworks under the Fourth Schedule of the GST Act, which exempts certain transactions for the purposes of GST.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Hong Kong, by comparison, which is major art market in the region, does not have a regime of goods and services or value-added taxes.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The result then is that it is often more cost-effective for art dealers to transact higher-value sales through Hong Kong than in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, local sales attract an additional GST charge.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I have been told, anecdotally, that this has been a long-standing issue for art gallerists in the visual arts space, as it makes large art deals hard to conclude in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A case can be made for the removal of GST in these instances; and it would not be the first time that this House and this Government would have granted such a thing.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The provision of financial services, sales of residential properties and, more recently, supplies of digital payment tokens, are just some examples of transactions that are presently exempt from GST.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There are technical reasons why financial services are exempt from GST; many other jurisdictions offer this exemption as well.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But I would like to highlight that in his 2012 Budget Statement, the then-Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance, Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam, introduced a GST exemption for investment-grade gold and other precious metals.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: He recognised that this exemption would, "facilitate the development of gold trading, which can draw on Singapore's strengths as an international financial centre and trading hub, to meet strong demand for investment-grade gold in Asia." I think what we can see is that where there are wider economic aims to be achieved, tax exemptions may be harnessed as a useful tool to grow important industries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The explanation for a GST hike next year is well-understood.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But, as the examples I have raised show, where there are wider aims to be achieved, such as the health of our creative economy and the livelihood of our creative professionals, tax exemptions may well be harnessed as a useful tool to grow what Singapore believes to be important industries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In its latest art market report, Art Basel and UBS noted that while performance was mixed across Asia for sales of post-war and contemporary art, Singapore was a notable exception.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This growth was said to be driven by the Sotheby's sale of modern and contemporary art, its first auction in the country after a 15-year hiatus.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: ART SG, the leading international art fair for Singapore and Southeast Asia, will return in 2024 for a second edition after a very successful run this year.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The point I would like to make is this: Singapore is home to excellent galleries, they exhibit to an international audience and are making sales to reputable institutions all over the world.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: And so, the question to be asked is this: how can we scale this to our advantage and make Singapore a world-class art trading hub?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A relook of our GST policy is, perhaps, one way to start.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The deduction also extends to donations of certain types of artefacts and pieces of public art.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In Ireland, artists themselves can enjoy an exemption from income tax on revenue derived from artistic works which are deemed to be original, creative works and which are generally recognised as having cultural or artistic merit.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Tax policies, such as those I have just mentioned, are just a very small selection of the economic tools that we have to stimulate demand in our art market, and I hope that what I have mentioned today gives the House an idea of some of the ways that structural economic incentives can be considered to support our creative industries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The next aspect of the creative economy that I would like to address, Mr Speaker, is the resilience and fortitude of the people who live and work in that economy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: One aspect of that resilience is the acquisition of a multidisciplinary skillset, one which enables artists to, in the words of the Arts Plan, "cross-pollinate" from within the creative economy to other adjacent industries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This multidisciplinary approach is something that is already being embraced by UAS.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The hope here is that by creating more avenues for our arts practitioners to acquire multidisciplinary skillsets, we diversify the economic opportunities and jobs available to these arts practitioners.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This approach is absolutely spot on, but we should be careful to frame this narrative in a responsible way as we move forward.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Many arts workers, and I count myself as one of them, we juggle portfolio careers to ensure that creative production is financially sustainable.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This means taking on job after job after job, very often with little respite.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The result is often emotional stress, mental burnout and, eventually, attrition.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: People with talent, passion and potential will leave the industry because they are exhausted and simply cannot afford to be in it any longer.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In a paper released in February 2019, Danish economics Prof Karol Jan Borowiecki analysed census data in the United States, which went back to 1850.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, in other words, the richer you are, the easier it is to sustain an artistic career.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a situation we must try to avoid at all costs.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Our arts producers must come from every sector of society, so that all types of subject matter and walks of life are well-represented.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It, therefore, follows that artists – all artists – must be able to earn a decent living from their practices.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Well, that brings me, Mr Speaker, to my last point, which is about education for art consumers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For the creative economy to thrive, the audience must value the products created by artists.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A common refrain that is heard amongst artists is why Singapore consumers will think nothing of spending thousands of dollars on designer handbags but will hesitate when it comes to spending similar amounts on works of local art.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Government to remember that, in addition to schools and institutions, working artists and independent art spaces also have a key role to play in educating the public about why art is necessary and about what good art is.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The latest Arts Plan refers to the conducting of Data Insights Clinics for arts Self-Employed Persons (SEPs) and arts organisations, and this is so that participants would be able to better understand the preferences of different audience segments.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While it is important for arts workers to produce works that are actually in-demand and will sell, we must not forget the value of the avant garde and the experimental in the arts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These kinds of works push boundaries and play an important role in challenging and educating audiences on art and cultural appreciation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Substation, for example, was and continues to be a safe space for experimental art to develop, although some might say its role is somewhat smaller now.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Independent art spaces, like Comma Space, Supper House, Starch, DECK and I_S_L_A_N_D_S Peninsula – these are just some examples of many, many small arts groups around that do important work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And indeed, the arts and culture are critical in fostering a more caring people, a cohesive society and a confident nation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The arts connect our communities to foster our identity as a people and as a nation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And it is this conviction in the role and the value of the arts has remained steadfast in the various masterplans that the Government has rolled out since the 1980s.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I shared with Members in this House in October 2020 that these plans have built a foundation for our nation's development and continued growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We strive to do more as our operating environment and our arts landscape evolve.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The recently launched Our SG Arts Plan 2023 to 2027, that Ms Usha Chandradas mentioned earlier, has this in mind as we seek to bring our flourishing arts sector to the next level.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have made significant shifts in how we support the arts, expanding from traditional forms to a more diverse and inclusive approach that embraces different artistic expressions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, on that note, I would like to highlight four areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With structured assistance, SEPs can better navigate their career path and acquire resilience, work experience and skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Just as supporting capability development in artistic excellence is always a priority, supporting the holistic growth of our arts practitioners is also critical.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Four years ago, in 2019, we launched the Arts Resource Hub (ARH) after very extensive consultations with our arts and culture practitioners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The ARH aims to help independent arts practitioners unlock new opportunities that Ms Usha Chandradas cited and access resources like wellness and welfare.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have also provided our arts SEPs with resources, such as talks on copyright, financial literacy, information on personal branding and well-being, as well as access to co-working spaces for sustainability practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will continue to review ARH to ensure that it serves the evolving needs of the arts SEPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In fact, this follows from my engagement session in February this year with a group of SEPs from the arts sector to discuss how we can better support them and how we can work together to co-curate solutions together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This identifies the occupations, job roles, training programmes, as well as existing and emerging skills that are required in arts education as well as technical theatre and production sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Looking ahead, I want to assure Ms Chandradas that the Government will certainly continue to support arts SEPs, strengthening their continuous education and training while providing different pathways for skills development and acquisition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Because by fostering a culture of lifelong learning and providing avenues for skills enhancement, we seek to empower our arts professionals to navigate their career landscape successfully.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Second, we are continuing to expand our arts infrastructure beyond presentation purposes, diversifying the spaces for artists and creatives to incubate, to experiment and to collaborate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Twenty years after we opened Esplanade Theatres on the Bay, we continue adding to Singapore's portfolio of first-rate performance and presentation spaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In fact, just last year, we inaugurated the Singtel Waterfront Theatre, a state-of-the-art venue with the grandeur and the technical capabilities to showcase our artists' talents on an international scale.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We also added the Singapore Art Museum (SAM) at Tanjong Pagar Distripark (TPD) to the growing pool of arts spaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This former industrial warehouse has really become a unique location for art showcases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Because of the voluminous gallery spaces accorded at TPD for the Singapore Biennale 2022, SAM was able to commission Singaporean artist Ong Kian Peng to develop an immersive audio-visual piece titled "The Viscous Sea", where viewers could experience the impact of climate change as they walk around the large-scale installation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I think this is really quite precious in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Today, under the Urban Redevelopment Authority's (URA) Community/Sports Facilities Scheme, we have seven co-located arts groups in commercial spaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: NAC also has a mix of small- and medium-sized venues for both creation and presentation purposes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We also look forward to the development of Kampong Java and, Ms Chandradas mentioned earlier, 45 Armenian Street, two work-in-progress spaces identified for artistic incubation, multidisciplinary experimentation and interdisciplinary collaboration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These new spaces are really part of our ongoing efforts to provide artists and audiences with various facilities and exciting opportunities to engage with the arts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They complement and enhance our arts scene, providing vibrant avenues and adding attractive aesthetics to our city.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To boost the development of our creative economy, we have injected strategic funds and rolled out targeted initiatives to support the growth of our arts and culture sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Ms Chandradas will remember the Arts and Culture Strategic Review in 2013, the CMF in 2014.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In fact, its $150 million top-up just last year, as well as the Arts and Culture Resilience Package in 2020, have all been instrumental in fortifying our arts and culture sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I want to assure Ms Chandradas and the House that MCCY and NAC will not let up our efforts in supporting the development of our arts practitioners and organisations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Looking ahead, we will find opportunities to support areas that reap synergies across the cultural as well as the creative sectors, strengthening the value proposition for the arts within the broader creative economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Beyond the Government grants, private sector giving and participation are, indeed, vital for a vibrant arts and culture landscape.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will continue to foster a breadth of private sector arts partnerships to nurture a culture of giving to the arts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Because of these generous contributions, we can support efforts such as Superhero Me's "One-on-One Mentorship to Market" programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is a programme that really tugs at the heartstring of a lot of people, because this fosters inclusion through the arts by partnering children with special needs with other children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The stART fund alleviated the concerns of Superhero Me organisers regarding startup costs, allowing them to quickly focus on enabling children with special needs to participate in artmaking and showcasing their works at the 2022 Singapore Writers Festival.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Last but not least, Ms Chandradas has highlighted that our creative economy needs audiences to thrive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Since the pandemic, new dynamics have emerged to reshape the relationship between artists and their audiences, for example, the change in consumption patterns from in-person attendance to hybrid platforms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To address this evolving landscape, it is crucial to understand the changes in audience preferences to regain audiences and to grow paying audiences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In this regard, we agree with Ms Chandradas' observation that there is a need to educate and, in fact, cultivate our audience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To that end, we recently launched the beta version of Catch.sg.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I hope Ms Chandradas has checked it out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is a one-stop digital platform aggregating arts and culture content in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It aims to drive audience attendance and enhance the accessibility of Singapore's arts and culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This initiative is led by NAC, with the support of the National Heritage Board, the Arts House Limited, National Gallery Singapore and Esplanade.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: More than 700 events from the arts community since September have enjoyed a boost in marketing since its launch and we are working to increase its local as well as international reach in the coming months through strategic partnerships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, Members of the House can look forward to catching up on our arts news when you take the SMRT trains or when you catch a Singapore Airlines flight.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And we want to thank all our partners for playing a role in broadening the reach of the arts in and beyond Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister of State, you have got about 30 seconds left.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, we are standing on a solid foundation to develop our creative economy to greater heights.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Since I have 30 seconds left, I have to pick and choose.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to work with Ms Chandradas and the sector on this.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Through the power of the arts, we can bring our people together.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We can inspire creativity and innovation and enrich lives.
